summaries.example: Imagine you see an apple and say, “It looks red.” Later, you learn that the light was unusual and the apple was actually yellow. Goodman says you might need to change even your first report about how it looked. Our observations are important, but they are not untouchable facts. We check them with other experiences and beliefs.
summaries.summary: Nelson Goodman was a philosopher who studied knowledge, language, science, logic, mathematics, and art. A main idea in this entry is anti-absolutism: Goodman did not think we begin with a tiny set of perfectly certain facts that can never be corrected. Even simple reports about experience may be revised when they do not fit with the rest of what we know. He also rejected a sharp division between statements true by meaning and statements learned from observation. In thinking about induction, or learning general lessons from examples, Goodman showed that the words we choose matter. His “grue” puzzle describes a color word that agrees with “green” for past observations but would predict blue after a chosen time. This suggests that not every description is equally good for making predictions. Goodman therefore emphasized fit, usefulness, simplicity, and the history of how words have been used. He was interested in many ways of making sense of things, rather than in one final, privileged description.
key_ideas: Goodman doubts that any small piece of experience is a perfect, unchangeable foundation for all knowledge.
People compare observations, rules, and beliefs and adjust them so they fit together better.
He questions the sharp line between truths that are true by meaning and truths learned from experience.
Different useful systems—such as science, philosophy, and art—can help us understand the world in different ways.
summaries.why_it_matters: Goodman’s ideas encourage careful thinking about evidence and language. They show that learning is not just collecting facts: we also decide which descriptions help us notice patterns and make sensible predictions. His work can help us understand why scientists revise theories, why different explanations may organize information differently, and why art can contribute to understanding as well as science.

important_terms.definition: The idea that some experiences are certain and cannot ever be corrected. Goodman challenges this idea.
A way of thinking that does not treat one final description as the only possible way to understand everything.
A statement or rule used to make predictions from examples. Some predicates work better for this than others.
The study of how parts fit together to make wholes.

questions_to_think_about: Can you remember a time when you changed your mind about something you saw or heard?
Should a rule be changed when it gives a surprising answer, or should the example be questioned first?
Can two different descriptions both help us understand the same thing?
Why might some words be better for making predictions than other words?

summaries.example: Suppose every emerald examined before time t is green. One may infer that all emeralds are green. But define “grue” as: examined before t and green, or examined at or after t and blue. The same past observations support the claim that all emeralds are grue, which predicts that the next newly examined emerald will be blue. “Green” and “grue” fit the evidence equally well up to t, yet they yield incompatible predictions. Goodman uses this case to argue that induction depends not only on evidence but also on which predicates are projectible.
summaries.summary: Nelson Goodman’s philosophy is organized around a rejection of absolute foundations and privileged representational frameworks. Against C. I. Lewis’s claim that phenomenal experience supplies an incorrigible “given,” Goodman argues that even apparently simple judgments about qualia—such as a remembered color experience—can be revised in light of a wider system of judgments. Their acceptance is therefore connected with overall coherence rather than guaranteed by an experience standing outside revision. Goodman also rejects a sharp analytic/synthetic distinction. His discussions of meaning favor extensional resources and lead toward likeness of meaning as a graded relation, rather than strict synonymy between distinct expressions. In logic and induction, Goodman treats ultimate justification as unavailable: rules are assessed together with considered inferential judgments in a process later called reflective equilibrium. His new riddle of induction then adds a further problem. “Green” and the temporally defined “grue” receive the same support from observations made before a selected time, while producing incompatible future predictions. Consequently, induction requires a distinction between projectible and non-projectible predicates. Goodman’s proposal connects projectibility with support, lack of violation or exhaustion, and comparative entrenchment—the extent to which predicates or related predicates have successfully figured in earlier projections. These themes extend into irrealism and worldmaking. Conflicting but adequate descriptions may correspond to different worlds or world versions, while science, philosophy, and art can all contribute to understanding. key_ideas: Goodman’s anti-foundationalism continues some logical-empiricist projects while rejecting an indubitable experiential base.
Judgments about experience are accepted within an interconnected system and may be revised when coherence with other judgments requires it.
Goodman argues that no sharp analytic/synthetic distinction is clearly available; likeness of meaning can be treated as a matter of degree rather than strict synonymy.
The old problem of induction cannot be solved by giving an ultimate justification of our inferential rules. Goodman instead emphasizes reflective equilibrium.
The new riddle of induction shows that identical past evidence can support incompatible predictions when expressed with different predicates.
Goodman’s irrealism and pluralism give an important role to multiple adequate world versions, constrained by coherence, simplicity, and entrenched usage.
summaries.why_it_matters: Goodman’s work matters because it links questions often treated separately: how experience supports knowledge, how language shapes generalization, and how different systems represent reality. The “grue” puzzle shows that evidence alone may not determine a prediction; the vocabulary used to describe evidence matters too. His approach also presents philosophical analysis as a practical reconstruction judged by structural fit, usefulness, and coherence rather than by a demand for perfect sameness of meaning or an ultimate foundation.

important_terms.definition: Goodman’s opposition to the idea that one absolute framework, foundation, or representation system must govern all legitimate knowledge.
The view that experience contains an indubitable foundation that cannot be revised. Goodman argues that even apparently simple experiential judgments may be reconsidered.
A predicate or hypothesis suitable for projection: using it in a generalization is supported by the relevant evidence and is not defeated by a better-established alternative.
A method of bringing accepted rules into better agreement with considered judgments by revising either the rules or the judgments when needed.
A theory of parts and wholes. Goodman uses mereological systems as an alternative to systems built from sets in some philosophical constructions.
The traditional contrast between truths based on meaning and truths based on experience. Goodman rejects a sharp, principled boundary between them.
Goodman’s view that conflicting true descriptions may correspond to different world versions, rather than all being descriptions of one uniquely structured world.
The use of a system of symbols or concepts to organize a description of reality. Goodman treats science, philosophy, and art as potentially significant representational practices.

questions_to_think_about: If every observation can in principle be revised, what distinguishes reasonable revision from arbitrary doubt?
Does reflective equilibrium justify rules, or merely describe how people settle on them?
Can a predicate be projectible because of its meaning alone, or does its history of use matter essentially?
If two world versions conflict, what standards can help us compare them without simply declaring one absolutely correct?
Does describing or naming a pattern help constitute it, or only help us notice something that already exists?

summaries.example: A class studies a pond and sees that every swan they have observed is white. They predict that the next swan will also be white. But someone invents the word “blite,” meaning white if seen before Friday and black if seen on Friday or later. Before Friday, every observed swan is both white and blite. The two words then support different predictions about later swans. Goodman’s puzzle asks why “white” seems like a better word for learning a general pattern than “blite.”
summaries.summary: Nelson Goodman was a major twentieth-century philosopher whose work ranged across logic, science, language, mathematics, and art. This entry presents him as an anti-absolutist: he did not believe that knowledge rests on an unquestionable foundation supplied by experience. For example, even a judgment about how something looked may need revision when it conflicts with other evidence. Instead of treating one observation as the final judge, we compare observations, beliefs, and rules and try to bring them into a good overall fit. Goodman also challenged the analytic/synthetic distinction, the supposed sharp division between statements true because of meaning and statements learned from experience. His most famous example for induction is the “grue” puzzle. Past evidence can support both an ordinary predicate such as “green” and a specially constructed predicate that agrees with it in the past but predicts a different future. This means that induction is not only about counting observations. It also depends on selecting predicates that are suitable for projection. Goodman explains this partly through entrenchment: predicates that have been used successfully in earlier generalizations are favored over unfamiliar or competing ones. He also studied systems for describing parts and wholes, and he developed a pluralist view of representation. Science, philosophy, and art may offer different ways of organizing understanding. These ways are not equally good merely because they are different: they remain subject to requirements such as coherence, simplicity, usefulness, and fit with accepted practice.
key_ideas: Goodman rejects the idea that some observations are completely protected from correction.
A belief is assessed together with other beliefs, evidence, and rules, not in isolation.
He argues that a perfectly sharp boundary between meaning-based truths and observation-based truths is not understandable or necessary.
The words used in a generalization affect whether the generalization gives a sensible prediction.
Past success makes some predicates more entrenched, or better established for future use, than others.
Goodman allows several useful world versions while still requiring them to meet standards such as coherence and simplicity.
summaries.why_it_matters: Goodman helps us see that reasoning depends on more than isolated facts. We must decide how to describe observations, which patterns are worth projecting into the future, and how different explanations fit together. His ideas are useful for thinking about scientific theories, changing one’s mind responsibly, and comparing different forms of understanding without assuming that one vocabulary automatically settles every question.

important_terms.definition: The view that knowledge does not rest on one final, unquestionable starting point. Beliefs can be checked and revised as a group.
The supposed certain starting point supplied by immediate experience. Goodman argues that even simple experience reports can be corrected.
A word or expression that describes things, such as “white,” “metal,” or “third son.”
A predicate that is appropriate for making a general prediction from observed cases.
The process of adjusting rules and judgments until they support one another in a stable way.
The difference between truths based on meanings and truths based on observations. Goodman doubts that this difference can be made sharp.
The study of how parts combine into wholes, used by Goodman in formal systems without relying on the same resources as set theory.
Goodman’s name for the view that different, well-supported ways of describing reality may correspond to different worlds or versions of worlds.

questions_to_think_about: If an observation conflicts with a well-supported theory, which should be revised?
Why does the choice of words matter when we generalize from examples?
Could two explanations disagree and still both be useful?
What makes a new way of describing something reasonable rather than random?
Is a rule reliable because it is logically certain, or because it has worked well with other judgments?
